' Mr. FORKE: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) the following question: I notice an in-

Cattle Shipments
terview in Saturday's Manitoba Free Press given by W. H. Forster of England, who came to Canada from England to purchase cattle. He intended purchasing about 2,000 head; he found when he came that all available space for ocean shipments had been contracted for.
It had been broadcast in England that Canada would have for sale this spring about twenty-five or thirty thousand head of cattle suitable for the British trade, and that the ocean freight would be about S15 per head. Now when a purchaser comes here, he finds all, or nearly all, space contracted for, and the ocean rate is $22.50 or $25 per head.
In view of the fact that the department has been urging farmers during the winter to have cattle ready for the market, had the department any knowledge that a condition such as exists might occur?
Mr. Speaker, it is difficult offhand to answer all these questions.
It is just one question.

But the answer to the one question does not do justice to the subject generally. My deputy is preparing a statement for the press that covers the whole question; it gives the sailings of all the steamers for the next four weeks from Montreal and St. John and shows that there will be a shortage of space for the first two weeks in May, that on the third week space will be equal to the demand, and that on the fourth week it will be greater than the demand. At the present time the space available is less than the demand. In a general way we had some information with regard to the number of cattle that would be shipped, but it was very difficult to get any exact figures. With the information furnished to us we have kept the shippers in Montreal acquainted with the requirements of this movement. That is all I can say in a verbal statement.
Is the minister aware of the fact that by the end of May the proper time for the shipment of this class of cattle is nearly past and space will be of little benefit to the shippers after that date?

Does my hon. friend think we should carry shipping space in our vest pocket ready for immediate requirements? There were two schools of thought apparent in Canada in connection with cattle shipments to Great Britain after the removal of the embargo: One was to deprecate the removal and to point out that there would be nothing much going over anyhow; the other was to exaggerate the movement. Between the two it was pretty difficult for us
to size up the situation. We kept the cattlemen fully supplied with information we gathered in regard to the situation. You cannot restore a trade that has been suspended for thirty years and expect to find everything ready for it3 resumption without some disturbance. Therefore it is quite natural that there should be a shortage of space for a brief period, but, as I have already indicated, in a few weeks there will be more than sufficient accommodation to meet the demand.

On the motion of Hon. W. S. Fielding (Minister of Finance) for Committee of Supply:
Mr. JOS. T. SHAW (Calgary West): 1 want to take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, of bringing to the attention of the House the application of the existing sales tax in so far as it affects public libraries. I am impelled to take this action at this particular time because I read in the public press that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is not averse to receiving suggestions from outside deputations with regard to the approaching budget, and it occurred to me that perhaps he might not be unwilling to view with favour suggestions made by members of this House.
Under the operation of the existing sales tax public libraries are subjected to a 6 per cent tax on books imported from foreign countries. And may I say at the outset that the majority of our books are imported? If these books are not imported directly they may be purchased, as they often are, from Canadian wholesalers, in which event a sales tax is charged the library of some 2i per cent; but in the price charged by the wholesaler is included the price which he must pay by way of sales tax, totalling 3| per cent. Therefore, in any event the library must pay a sales tax of 6 per cent on its purchases.
Another factor that is of great importance to public libraries is the matter of bindings, which they use very considerably. Bindings are subject to a sales tax of 4J per cent. Now, it is rather a strange coincidence that while libraries have been exempted so far as their purchases are concerned from the operation of the customs tariff, they have not been exempted from the sales tax in their purchases of books and bindings. The operation of this sales tax, as I have indicated, constitutes a very grievious burden to public libraries. There is, as must be matter of common knowledge, an increasing demand on public libraries to-day, and it is also a fact that these institutions are receiving decreased appropriations. In the city from which I come we have a very efficient tax-supported public library officered by a very capable official indeed, a library which serves not only our city but a very large surrounding country. In the city of Calgary alone the operation of the sales tax during the present fiscal year will mean the payment by that library of about $1,000. During the year also there has been a decrease in the appropriations for this library totalling $2,000, In the western provinces the operation of the sales tax will mean
approximately $10,000 to public libraries, of which amount $7,000 represents the tax on the purchase of books alone.
I hold in my hand a letter from the Inspector of Libraries for the province of Ontario, and I should like to indicate his views in connection with this matter. Referring to the libraries in Ontario, he says:
Our libraries expended in that year $164,185.
That is, the year 1921. Continuing, he
says:
The sales tax is a heavy burden on our libraries. The prices of books have increased tremendously since before the war, and the libraries' incomes are decidedly limited. The Dominion government has always recognized the general public service of public libraries by permitting imported books to come to the public libraries free of duty. Surely the sales tax should be removed when it is in the general public's good that it should be removed. The Ontario legislature bases its grants largely on book purchases, and we find that our grants are not as effective by reason of the tax that is imposed ?
It is apparent, therefore, to anyone who ponders the situation for a moment that the tax-supported public libraries find themselves ground between the millstones of heavy federal taxation on the one hand and a decreasing appropriation on the other, the latter due primarily to the financial stringency. While the tax does bear very seriously upon the individual library, I think it can fairly be said that the aggregate amount received by the government, so far as the application of the tax to libraries is concerned, is very insignificant indeed.
The special objection which I have to the particular tax that I am referring to is that it constitutes a tax upon taxation. This is a case of double taxation, and falling as it does upon a tax supported institution, it bears very heavily indeed. Strange to relate, when the statute was drawn the provincial libraries were specially exempted, but other public libraries, equally tax-supported, were not favoured with exemption. Under these circumstances I am asking the House in the form of a resolution to indicate that this tax should be removed, in its application to public libraries in so far as it affects the purchase of books and of binding supplies.
I know that I shall be met with one or two arguments. It will be suggested. I doubt not, that the matter should first be taken up with the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) or the Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Bureau). But the library officials last year did take the matter up not only with the Minister of Finance but with the Minister of Customs and Excise, and they did not accomplish their desire. It will be urged, also, I assume, that to move an amendment when going into Coni-

Sales Tax
mittee of Supply constitutes a vote of want of confidence in the government. I have not any desire by this vote to indicate any such want of confidence so far as this particular item is concerned. I do want to suggest however, that there has not been any other opportunity to bring this matter to the attention of the House. Had I brought it up by way of private member's resolution I should have been met with the suggestion that it constituted in effect a subtraction of the public revenue and consequently would not be legal under that head. Bringing it up at this time, I may be met with the suggestion, as I have said, that it is a vote of want of confidence. Well, it is about time that hoary tradition was dispensed with; and I notice that in the Mother of Parliaments itself, the most transparent technicality has lately been taken advantage of in order to obviate the application of that rule. Then again, it may be urged, "Why not bring it up in the budget debate?" But if ever there was a time for pious platitudes, surely it is when the budget is under consideration, I do suggest to the government that this is the time and this is the place to bring to the attention of parliament a matter which to my mind is of vital significance to our public libraries and also to the reading public.
But I may be met further with the argument: "Why pick out this particular item? Why single out the sales tax in its application to public libraries? Why not deal with a dozen other things?" Well, I want to say at the outset that the tax in its effect upon libraries is particularly vicious, particularly harmful. It is, as I have pointed out, a tax upon taxation; it is in a category by itself so far as sales tax is concerned. And not only that: while I have very serious objection to the sales tax in many directions, I sometimes think it is much more desirable to attack the enemy in detail rather than by making a' frontal attack. I feel, that it is going to be a great many years before we shall have in vogue in ' this country a proper, scientific system of taxation. No effort has yet been made to delimit, if you like, the various fields of taxation-Dominion, provincial, and municipal. Consequently I must take this opportunity of presenting to the House a resolution dealing with this particular matter. I move in amendment:
That all the words in the resolution after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
Whereas public libraries are necessary and valuable educational institutions not existing for profit and supported by public taxation,
And whereas, on account of the increasing demand for library facilities and the difficult economic conditions prevailing, public libraries in Canada are experiencing the greatest difficulty in financing their reasonable requirements,
And whereas the application of the sales tax on the purchases of books and book-binding by public libraries constitutes a heavy financial burden, limiting the usefulness and impairing the efficiency of such public libraries,
Therefore be it resolved that this House deems it advisable that public libraries in Canada, supported by public taxation, be exempted from the operation of the sales tax in so far as the same affects the purchases of books and book-binding by such public libraries.
The amendment is seconded by the hon. member for McLeod (Mr. Coote).

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the question of nonconfidence to which the hon. gentleman has referred I am reminded of the old lines, "It was all very well to dissemble your love, but why did you kick me downstairs?" I do not want to dwell on the question of non-confidence. I think I have a better reason for asking my hon. friend not to press his motion, or if he is to press it, for asking the House not to accept it.
With what he has said as to the importance of public libraries, the desirability of encouraging them and the hard times they are perhaps having, I am sure I can heartily sympathize, as I am sure most members of the House will, but that is by no means a conclusive reason why we should adopt this motion. I am not at the moment expressing any opinion whether it is or is not desirable that we should exempt public libraries from the sales tax. This is but one of twenty questions which are being presented to the government by hon. members on both sides of the House. I am sure I am probably within my facts when I say that I see before me on the two portions of the opposite benches at least a score of gentlemen who have done me the honour of calling upon me to impress upon me some particular thing in which they would like some reduction of taxation or some exemption from the operation of this or that tax. One gentleman here on this side of the House makes a habit of urging the exemption from the income tax where there are a certain number of children. Another hon. member brings forward some particular thing in which he is sincerely desirous of having a change, and no doubt they could all make a measure of popularity if they would get up in this House and become the champion -of this or that particular thing. But why should we select among these fifty or more things-perhaps I had
Sales Tax

better be moderate and say among the twenty or more changes proposed:-why pick out of the basket this particular thing and ask the judgment of the House upon it this afternoon? I fail to see the reason. I had a large deputation the other day urging very strongly that in the matter of income tax any man who contributes to charity or religion or any of the various noble causes which we are all asked to help should not be taxed on what he contributes for that purpose. That is perhaps as strong a case as my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Shaw) brings forward, but all who have these things in mind have been content to make their case and await the moving of the waters. I know of no reason why this particular case or fad, if I may dare call it that, and not offensively, for fads are good things at times, should be selected for us to vote upon to-day. If it is good policy to do that, then hon. gentlemen opposite-I am not designating any member-who have come before me and asked that a particular tax be abolished ought to get up and move in the same way and somebody else move for income tax exemption where there are children. Each of these things may be important in itself, but I submit to the House there is no good reason why we should pick out this particular thing and ask the House to pass judgment upon it this afternoon.
The sales tax is not a particular baby of my own. It was a system, and probably a necessary system, established by the forme.-government. I have had the unpleasant duty of increasing the amount of it. That is my crime in the matter. When the late government devised the tax I know that they made many exemptions; some people think too many; I know there is something to be said against exemptions. But the late government did make a very liberal list of exemptions. They considered public libraries I have no doubt, and no doubt thought that taken all in all libraries could stand the tax as well as many other things. I am not declaring against the judgment of the hon. member for Calgary. I am asking him to consider whether it is wise to ask the House to select this particular one out of the many questions, anticipate the budget, and ask for a vote upon it now. I do not think that is fair. I do not think either party in the House should accept the motion.
Amendment negatived.

Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I 
would like to call the attention of the Acting Postmaster General (Mr. Graham) to a matter concerning which I should have spoken when the House was in supply, but being occupied in a committee of the House I was unable to do so. It is regarding the special delivery of letters, on which a stamp of twenty cents has now to be placed. Many complaints have reached me from Montreal on this subject, and I would like to call the attention of the acting minister to the matter so that he may investigate it.
When the special delivery was originally devised, the postage was fixed at ten cents; it is now twenty cents, in addition to the three cents ordinary postage. That makes twenty-three cents for a special delivery letter. Last Thursday I had occasion to send a special delivery letter to Montreal,. placing twenty cents postage on it. The letter was wrongly delivered, but I am not complaining of that, as the address might not have been as perfect as it should have been.
I would ask hon. gentlemen to kindly refrain from conversation while the hon. member is addressing the House.

Montreal is now a very large city and it includes many outlying municipalities. When a special delivery letter, bearing a twenty-cent stamp in addition to the usual postage stamp, is brought into the post office it is handed over to a boy who is paid eight cents to deliver the letter in any part of the city which is served by the Montreal general post office. The government has received twenty-three cents from this letter and pays only eight cents to the messenger for its delivery. By common knowledge in the Montreal post office these messenger boys are the worst paid in the service, and I would ask the minister even if he cannot reduce the taxation on letters to at least give some encouragement to these messengers and grant them a better remuneration than they are receiving at the present time. Because these boys may have to go, in the course of their journeys, to almost the extreme end of the island of Montreal to deliver one of these letters for eight cents; they spend practically the best part of the forenoon and afternoon and are even employed late in the evening, at this work. If the ordinary postage rate is going to be reduced, at any time, from three to two cents, I would ask the government to consider whether it would not be possible to revert to the old rate of ten cents for special delivery letters from the present rate of twenty cents, and thereby increase the use of this facility which is not as well resorted to at the present time as it used to be in the old days. It provides also for the travelling expenses of investigating officers, for legal expenses in connection with the rejection of immigrants and other miscellaneous and incidental expenses, not chargeable to any specific service.
We spent on this service $125,000, and we are asking for an increase of $15,000 making $140,000.
Postage, telegrams, cablegrams, telephone express and freight charges in Canada, $25,000. This is to meet the cost of postage on parcels and letters addressed to
[Mr. C. A. Stewart.
points outside of Canada; for cablegrams, telegrams, long distance telephone tolls, freight and express charges on books, manifests, forms, stationery supplies, immigration literature and maps, etc., shipped to points in Canada and outside of Canada.
Inspection of British immigrant children, $15,000.
This is to provide for the cost of inspection of children emigrating to Canada under the auspices of the various homes and societies in the British Isles, these children being placed in Canadian farmers' homes. What arrangements are made for the children on this side of the water?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: So far we are utilizing the various organizations that have been engaged in this work. I gave a list of them when the vote was going through. In most cases though not in all, they have foster homes already located for those children. We are making inquiry as best we can, and as soon as possible after the child is settled we will make an inspection to ascertain the desirability of the home and what success is being made with the settlement of the child in the particular home.
You continue making inspection from time to time in this connection?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, if possible, twice a year.

The minister spoke of
special writers. What jurisdiction or supervision does the department exercise over these special writers?

speechtext: They are people who write special articles for advertising purposes which must pass the officer of the department who is in charge of publicity, Mr. Stead. Seaport agencies and detention hospitals and halls expenses, $85,000. This is to cover the cost of administration and maintenance of agencies and offices at the various seaports: St. John, Halifax, Quebec, Montreal, Vancouver, Victoria, New York, Boston. It also provides for the equipment, administration and maintenance of immigration detention hospitals and halls at St. John, Halifax,. Quebec, Montreal, Vancouver and Victoria. The above expenses consist of cost of uniforms, telegrams, cablegrams, telephones, freight and express charges, wages of cleaners; travelling expenses of officers attached to these agencies; laundry, charwomen for the cost of board of immigrants temporarily detained for medical observation on account of minor contagious diseases, etc.
So far as detention while under medical inspection is concerned most of these charges are recovered, because in nine cases out of ten it is the fault of the medical officer on board the ship that proper inspection had not taken place prior to embarkation, and in every case in which that occurs the steamship companies are required to pay the cost while the patients are detained for medical attention in those hospitals, or until such time as they return to the country from which they came. This amount is about the same as we have had in former years. The memorandum continues:
In land agencies and maintenance of immigration halls in the West, $20,000.
This item is to provide for the expenses of our various inland agencies throughout Canada, and for the maintenance of immigration halls at certain points in the. West, and especially at our agency at Winnipeg. These expenses consist of cost of uniform, telegrams, telephones, freight and express charges, wages of cleaners, food for deports and immigrants temporarily detained in the immigration buildings, laundry, pillows, blankets, and other expenses necessary for general upkeep and maintenance.
The expenditure for 1921-22 was $12,696 and for the
eleven months ending February 28, 1923, $12,485.
Deportation expenses amount to $50,000. This is to cover the travelling expenses of the deportation officers, the cost of uniforms, and meals for deports on train, rail and steamship fares, in cases where the railroad and steamship companies are not liable for free transportation. The increase is due to the fact that by agreement with the Department of Health aliens convicted under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act and ordered to be deported have to be handled by this department under the provisions of the Immigration Act. Up to last year it was not the duty of the Immigration department to do this work but now
all persons convicted under the Narcotic Drug Act and who are to be deported are handed over to the officers of this department. Frankly, I sometimes think that this is rather the duty of the Dominion police than of the Immigration department. However, for the time being we are performing this service.
The next item is $50,000 for boundary inspection expenses. It is to provide for the cost of uniforms of boundary inspection officers- as well as to pay for meals, lodging and travelling expenses, for relieving inspectors and for overtime on Sundays and statutory holidays. It also provides for the incidental upkeep of offices on the boundary line between. the United States and Canada. In 1921-22, we spent $42,785.06 and for the eleven months ending February 28, 1923, we expended $51,955.62. We therefore expect to get along with a little less this year than we did last year.
For contingencies and general expenses ir the United States the vote is $180,000. This item is to provide for the expenses of nineteen agencies maintained and operated in the United States. These expenses consist of rent of offices, furniture, typewriting machines, postage, telegrams, telephone messages, freight, express charges, light and fuel, stationery supplies, printing envelopes, cards and letterheads, and temporary assistance, and to provide for the salaries of fifteen new field men. The expenses in connection with this field work are estimated to be in the neighbourhood of $50,000 for the year. I have some doubt as to two items here, this and the next one. When the items were inserted I did not know what difficulties would be encountered in the appointment of these agencies. What I intended to do was to revive the old system of getting farmers who had been successful in Canada to go to the United States and Great Britain and lecture during the winter months, but our Civil Service Act makes it somewhat difficult to carry out appointments of this kind. They would not be permanent, and you could scarcely call them temporary. So that there is considerable difficulty in making such appointments, and I intend to cut down the amount in connection with this work so that we shall need only three or four lecturers to go to the Old Country; and I shall abandon my intention of sending any to the United States.
Would it not be difficult to get farmers who are successful to go abroad?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Not at all, any number of them. We are asking for

Supply-Immigration

$50,000 for field work in the United States, and $75,000 for Great Britain.
Then there is an item for contingencies and general expenses on the continent. This is to provide for expenses to be incurred in connection with equipment and maintenance of seven or eight officers in Europe to vise passports and see to the inspection of immigrants coming to Canada. The expenses will include rent, furniture, fuel, light, taxes, uniforms, inspection, freight and ^express charges, postage, telegrams, cablegrams, telephone service, salaries of temporary employees, typewriting .machines, stationery and supplies, books, letterheads, travelling expenses, etc. I might say that this is entirely a new service which is being carried on on the continent of Europe. We have offices located at Antwerp and Warsaw, and we hope to be established in Prague. Our officers will travel to three or four other points to make inspections of people embarking on steamships and to advise them as to whether or not they are likely to be accepted in Canada on inspection. We do not, of course, guarantee that they shall be permitted to land, but we see to it that they shall have a fair idea ns to whether or not they will be admitted. We are rapidly getting past the point where we find it necessary to reject people on account of the occupational test. Indeed, that difficulty no longer exists in regard to the northern countries of Europe, and not at -all so far as Great Britain and the United States are concerned. This work is intended to apply only to people on the continent of Europe outside of the territory I have mentioned. We shall admit from the continent only domestic servants, farm labourers and those who can engage in farming; in other words, those who can buy farm lands. Our object is to obviate what has occurred in the past and has caused a great deal of hardship to people who upon landing at St. John, Quebec, or any of the other ports of Canada, find that they are not permitted to enter the country. I am told that on one occasion there were as many as 2,000 persons kept in detention and sent back to the country of their origin because they could not be permitted to land under the regulations. Last year, on the other hand, we never had at any one time more than five, and I hope that that condition will continue. This vote of $100,000 is an entirely new one and is experimental; and if we find that it is not warranted, then, of course, we shall withdraw the officers. I do think, however, that it will be of great advantage in preventing people from coming to Canada who have

no chance of getting in. Such people might otherwise be unable to obtain adequate information regarding the conditions and the regulations, and we shall at least see that they do not make an unnecessary trip across the ocean.
The next vote is also a new one. It is one which I dealt with when speaking to the House on a previous occasion. It is to provide for the work of repatriating Canadians who left eastern Canada particularly. We have not been active in the eastern field, having had agencies only at BostQn and Manchester. We are asking for a vote of $20,000 for the purpose of repatriating those Canadians who have left eastern Canada, as we think a useful work could be done in endeavouring to bring these people back into this country. This is to provide for the salaries and travelling expenses of colonization agents and to meet the necessary expenditures involved in connection with the work of bringing back into Canada those people who have gone abroad, especially French-Canadians. The expenses consist chiefly in travelling and living expenses of those engaged in this undertaking, and also provides for halls for lecture purposes, etc. It is intended to make a special effort in this field during the year 1923-24. The next item relates to the Women's Immigration Division. We are asking for $15,000 to provide for the expenses of conductresses on trains of parties of girls coming to Canada to engage in domestic service, and also to pay for salaries and uniforms for these women officers and to provide grants for women's hostels maintained in the principal cities in Canada, for temporary assistance and welfare of immigrant women, and for a per diem allowance of $1.50 to these free hostels for accommodation accorded by them to women immigrants coming into Canada to engage in domestic service, such free accommodation not to extend in any case over more than forty-eight hours; also for travelling expenses of women officers and of ladies attending the annual reunion or convention of the Canadian Council of Immigration. Then we have grants to immigration or colonization societies. We propose to increase the grant to the Salvation Army by $10,000, as they intend extending their work very materially in connection with domestic servants. To the Scottish Aid Society we are maldng a grant of $5,000. This is a new organization working in the north of Scotland, headed by the Reverend Father Macdonald, and supported by such prominent men as Mr. Burns and Mr. McBrien. Father Macdonald has been actively engaged in this work for a

Will the minister be good enough to let us have any more information than he may have on that particular subject?

speechtext:
I think I gave the committee when the matter was under discussion before the names of those connected with the organization. Lest I forget, before leaving the matter of publicity, there is one very important feature that I must mention. We have an arrangement both in Canada and in Great Britain under which the transportation companies and the government have formed a publicity committee. This committee is for the purpose of preventing overlapping and getting full value for the expenditure on publicity, and to this end various fields of advertising are allocated to particular parties. This committee will co-ordinate our whole publicity campaign. . I think I covered most of the field the other day in connection with the Canada Colonization Association. 2.	Lands and location to be subject to inspection to determine suitability and fix maximum prices-this to be undertaken either by the provincial or Dominion government.
In answer to my hon. friend I may say that the Manitoba government have expressed their willingness to undertake this work. This is not true of the other two prairie provinces and it would have to be undertaken by a representative of the Soldiers' Settlement Board. In 50 per cent of the cases this board already have the values fixed upon lands adjacent to the railways, because I do not think it would be good business to permit the sale of lands at any distance from the railways, particularly where we are giving government assistance in the way of helping any organization to perform this service.

Five.	[DOT]

3.	The association agrees that all moneys received from subscribers, commissions on sales of land, or government grants, will be utilized to carry on settlement work.

It is the

Brunswick. In rising to discuss the issue to-day I prefer to deal more with the general question of immigration rather than with any particular item. I had the misfortune of being indisposed during the major portion of this debate, but I have read with care the contributions to the debate by the various members taking part in it. I have no apology to offer to the House for discussing at some little length, although it may be tedious, this question of immigration into Canada. It is undoubtedly the paramount question, of transcendent importance to this country, Considering the economic circumstances and financial conditions in which Canada stands to-day this is a very, very important question going really to the root of our economic existence, being second only in importance to that of confederation itself. Therefore the subject is worthy of long and careful debate. I spoke on this question last year at some length, and I propose to speak on it at some length again to-day.
What are the problems that are facing this government? When the government came into power the question of constitutional liberty was at stake. That was disposed of by the accession of this government to office, but on coming into office the government was faced with outstanding problems of an economic nature. This government has a business proposition to meet. There is a tremendous indebtedness hanging over the heads of the people of Canada to-day, amounting in the total to something like four billions of dollars That includes the national debt, provincial and municipal indebtedness. It does not touch the individual indebtedness, the money owed h}' the various citizens of the country.
The second great economic problem facing us is the railroad problem. Last year we went back some seventy-two or seventy-three million dollars on that account. This year in spite of a wonderful harvest in western Canada that probably saved the railroads, we went back some sixty million dollars.
The third great problem, which is subsidiary to the other two, is to alleviate the burden of taxation on the shoulders of our citizens and to give to this present generation in Canada a fair and moderate means of living. There is no question that the whole world

to-day, the citizens of every country are groaning under a heavy burden of taxation. We in this country must expect no odds. Whatever advantage we may take of the circumstances, we shall still have to bear a very-heavy load. The cost of the war must be paid and we in this generation must pay our share of it. This country faces a tremendous problem, as great a problem as Canadians ever faced.
The building of the Canadian Pacific railway in Canada was something that tested the metal of our people. To-day Canadians have a real and genuine test to undergo. I do not know how this burden of taxation can be relieved-how our people can be relieved from the heavy burdens that rest upon them, how industry can be relieved from heavy taxation-unless, by some means or other, there is created in this country a large amount of wealth that can be taxed. You can pass acts of parliament but parliamentary enactments will not create wealth; wealth can only be created by the application of labour to our natural resources. That must be done if we of this generation are to escape the tremendous burden that rests upon us. Supposing there had been a crop failure in western Canada last year-western Canada that has contributed six or seven hundred millions of dollars to the general body of wealth in this country? Had there been a crop failure last year our position would have been immeasurably worse than it is to-day. That may come, probably will come-we cannot expect a bountiful harvest all the time-and if it should come our position would be bad. The only way that we can possibly meet the situation is by creating wealth in this country.
The natural resources of Canada are great. It is almost tautological to repeat of what these resources really consist. ' There is land in this country of great fertility; there are some two hundred million acres suitable for agriculture that are as yet untilled. We have vast forests, which are yielding us to-day some $200,000,000 per annum. As to mines we are, as yet, only on the fringe of their development. The stage is set in Canada to-day to take care of a population of thirty millions. We have the railroads, we have the telephones, we have the telegraphs, we have the shipping lines, we have the canals, we have the elevators built far beyond the needs of our present population. Why? Because we are a widely scattered people. This National railway of ours, which showed a deficit this year of $60,000,000, has contiguous to it a great area of fertile country. It runs, probably, through the best area of fertile country served

by any transcontinental railroad on the American continent. Between the city of Winnipeg and the city of Edmonton, within a distance of ten miles on each side of the railroad, there is asserted by competent authorities to be some ten or twelve million acres of untilled arable land.
Will the hon. gentleman elucidate a little further his point as to the elevators being beyond the needs of the country at the present time?

I will come to that later on. In northern Ontario there is asserted to be in the clay belt some twenty-five million acres of arable land. Those who have not seen that district would be well repaid by travelling over the railway which passes through it. Last year I went up into that country at the close of the session, and I saw white clover covering the hills down to the railroad track for miles. Where that clover flourishes agriculture will also thrive. The Canadian Pacific railway, which has grown to greatness on account of the land immediately adjacent to it and by reason of the development of the west, runs through a country which is comparatively poor compared with that-which is traversed by the Transcontinental railway. The clay belt through which the latter railway runs will, in years to come, prove to be agricultural land of fine quality. North of lake Superior the Canadian Pacific passes through a rocky country. In the far West the land through which that railway runs is more or less drought stricken. On the other ltand, the Transcontinental and Grand Trunk Pacific run through a country which is well wooded and well watered.
Where is the solution of the problem which confronts us to be found? If we have these resources, and no one can deny that they exist, what is it that we lack? We are simply short of man power to create that wealth of which I have spoken. Have we come to such a position in Canada to-day that we cannot bring together the two forces that are necessary to create that wealth? We have great natural resources, with all the appliances necessary for their development, and the man power can be got from the teeming populations of Europe. Can we get that man power that we need so much? Undoubtedly we can. The United States has had to close her doors against immigration-immigration that built up Canada in the past. In the last analysis Canada was built up by immigrants; we are all immigrants or the descendants of immigrants. In the cities of Canada to-day there are hundreds, yes thousands, of
men versed in agricultural pursuits who could go on the land and work it if a proper policy were inaugurated to enable them to do so. Shortly before I came away I addressed an audience in my own constituency and spoke upon the question of immigration, a question of deep interest to those people, and a man rose in the meeting and said "There are two or three hundred of us here." Those people were Germans of the very sturdiest and finest stock of agriculturists that Canada ever had. He went on to say "If we were given that chance we would go out and we could make a success of farming. One thing we are short of is capital." I think you could go through the cities of Canada and gather together men and women who to-day are merely existing, who are agriculturists by profession but are to-day competing with labour in these urban centres, who would be glad to go on the land where they could produce wealth to the advantage of themselves and to the advantage of Canada as a whole. As a result of the Great War and the dislocation of economic and industrial affairs in Europe I believe there are to be found there to-day men and women of good calibre, the very best types that the countries of Europe have, agriculturists by profession, who have been broken, probably ruined, as a result of the great conflict. If these were brought to Canada they would be a great acquisition to the country.
What may we expect immigration to do for Canada? What did immigration do fbr Canada in the past? In the early years of the history of Ontario immigration, in the course of fifty or one hundred years, turned a wooded wilderness into a wonderful land. Many of the early settlers who came to the province of Ontario were disbanded soldiers of the agricultural immigrant type. Irish and Scotch soldiers who formed a large percentage of the British army. They came from peasant stock, they cleared the land; they remained where they settled; they never talked of leaving Canada; they built up a great province. The same is true of the provinces of Quebec, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. Whenever we brought the real agricultural immigrant to this country he stayed. The settlers who have -not remained in this country, in my opinion, were not of the real agricultural type.
What did immigration do for western Canada? When Clifford Sifton became Minister of the Interior and took charge of immigration in this country it was as if a wizard had waved its wand over the land. In western Canada everything was in a state of stagnation. In the eastern parts of Canada, including cities, a similar condition prevailed. In a few years

The cities of Canada began to grow and I tell you, Mr. Chairman, it was as a result of that policy and that policy alone, that the cities of western Canada were built up, and that the great grain industry of western Canada was developed, the growth of which is one of the marvels of the world. When Clifford Sifton commenced his immigration policy the province of Saskatchewan was producing some

The harbour of Montreal was choked with grain vessels last year solely because of that immigration policy. There is a real connection between that immigration policy and the growth of the great manufacturing cities of Ontario and Quebec. We need an immigration policy to-day far more than in the days of Clifford Sifton. At that time we could pick and choose. We were not burdened with debt. We were not under financial difficulties. We had a great country. We merely needed it opened up for the creation of wealth. But to-day we need more than that. We stand in such economic peril that an immigration policy is an economic necessity, and we are not in a position to-day to say that we will pick and choose. What we want to-day is a man who can make his way in the country. His passport must be his capacity to get through. As James Fitzjames% said when challenged by the Highland chief:
My pass in danger tried
Hangs in its sheath and by my side.
The qualification of the immigrant into this country is his capacity to earn an honest living and to wrest it from the soil by toil and labour What has been happening in regard to immigration in this country in the last few years? To-day I am expressing my own ideas. I am not speaking in condemnation of the government, but I must say immigration has fallen away and fallen away badly. At the outbreak of the war there was an immigration of some 380,000 a year. In the year ended March, 1921, there was immigration of
148.000,	and in the year ended March last the figure was 89,000.
Now, what is the policy of other nations situated as we are? New Zealand, Cape Colony and Australia have adopted a genuine policy of going to Great Britain and Europe, securing immigrants and settling up and developing their country. To-day the immigration of Australia is its biggest feature. There
fMr. McMurray.]
is a national spirit behind it, and it is backed with the national wealth. I think that should be the policy of this country. That is the policy that has the good will of the
5 p.m. Canadian people behind it, and that is the policy into which we should put our. money.
If I were passing any criticism on the particular items under consideration. I would say they are too small. They should be multiplied by ten, and that the great desideratum for the consideration of this government, should be the creation of wealth in this country that will protect us and our children from the hardships under which we and they must exist. To the men of eastern Canada, of Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton, London, I would say that their manufacturing and commercial existence are at stake if wealth is not created in their great markets of western Canada. Anything that is injurious to that great market of eastern Canada, the great market being western Canada, reacts directly and instantly upon the manufacturing and commercial centres of eastern Canada, and it should be the policy of eastern Canada to do everything in its power to make conditions so that wealth can be produced readily and easily on the plains of the West. I would say to the people of western Canada, and to their representatives in this House, that unless you bring more people into this country to create a larger body of wealth to help to bear your burden, you cannot expect to get a reduction in tariff. How can you expect to get a reduction in railroad rates? This indebtedness of Canada must be met. It cannot be repudiated. If you do not create that body of wealth, if you do not bring more shoulders to bear the burden, then you yourselves must bear it. It is in vain to think you can throw it down and repudiate it. If you want lower taxes, then there is only one solution-bring in the thousands of immigrants that can be added to the population of western Canada. Let them till your fertile land, let them help to bear your burdens. We are not bringing these people here as servants or slaves. We are bringing them to a country where the national burden individually per capita is probably much lower than in any other country in the world, the United States being the only country I can think of where the national burden per capita is lower than in Canada. The majority of these immigrants are coming from a place of dire distress to a country not where money can be conjured up or created, but where honest, hard toil is rewarded fairly well, where they and their countrymen and countrywomen before them have done

How does the hon.
member propose to settle all the thousands of people on the land unless they have the money to buy it? When the hon. member speaks of the power behind the immigration policy, the national wealth, does he suggest the financing of these people in the purchasing of the land?

If the hon. member will be patient I will try to come to that in due course of time and will illustrate what I think could be done. Probably the hon. member will not agree with me, and probably few in the House will agree with me, but I am taking the opportunity of putting my ideas forward on a question that I think is of paramount importance to the whole of Canada and- of transcendent importance in western Canada.
Who should these immigrants be? In my opinion the immigrants that should be brought to this country ought to be in the first instance agriculturists? I would not close the door to any immigrant who has the hardihood and the courage to cross the ocean to come to this country, but I would make a strong bid for men and women who can develop the resources of the country. And who are they? They are the sort of people who in the past made a success in Canada; they are the people who bettered their own conditions and therefore proved valuable and useful settlers in Canada. I am going to deal largely with western Canada, because it is of western Canada that I know most, having lived some twenty-six years on its plains. In the early days I drove over most of it on horseback and buckboard and I knew its people of the old time. I know the old time rancher and the large'grain grower, and I know the people who have lived in the cities of that part. of the country as well as the men on the frontiers. It is therefore of the development of that West, which I have seen unrolled like a panorama before me during some twenty-six years, that I wish to speak to-day.
I will deal, if I may, with the question of the financial conditions existing in western Canada as set forth at considerable length by some of my Progressive friends in this House. The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Mac-Kelvie), speaking in this House the other day, suggested our keeping away from the people of central and southern Europe. The majority of us who have lived in western Canada, and I believe the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) particularly will join me in an encomium of those people of southern and
central Europe for the contribution that they have made in labour and toil to the development of that part of our Dominion. The policy of Sir Clifford Sifton brought to western Canada the Ukrainians, many of whom came in their sheepskin coats and in their quaint European dress; and to-day in the University of Manitoba .20 per cent of the students are the descendants of those people of central Europe. The same is true in regard to the Agricultural College in Winnipeg, and I believe the same truth holds in Saskatchewan. I had the pleasure of travelling on the train with a leading educationist of Saskatchewan and he told me of two boys whom he had taught in a small schoolhouse near the town of Yorkton and both of whom are Ukrainians and to-day, university men. AVe have numbers of lawyers among these people, and the professions are filling up with them. They make good Canadians; they are the very best citizens; and I have never known in the hard two or three years that we have passed through in recent times of any of these people asking charity from municipality, provincial government or Dominion government.
Has the member for North Winnipeg consulted the statistics of the Social Bureau of Winnipeg?
I have looked over those statistics, and the men we call "foreigners" were largely conspicuous by their absence.
I agree with the hon. gentleman in a general way, but a certain percentage of them undoubtedly sought relief.

What I said was that I had not known of any of them who had done so. These people were settled in western Canada in some of the very poorest parts of the country, as iny hon. friend for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) can bear me out. In his constituency they were settled in low swampy land out around Beausejour. The land was drained, the trees cut and the place was developed. Crops were produced and that section of the country was turned practically into an agricultural garden. This year I was near the town of Neepawa and along the mountain the grain was turning golden for miles and miles, so that one beheld a beautiful agricultural scene. That land was owned by Ukrainians who came to the country practically without a dollar; but by patient and diligent toil they built up a paying industry for themselves. A collector for a large machine company told me that he was able to collect far more money from these Ukrainian people than he could from the English,

Canadian and American settlers. He could get ten times as much from these people, and apparently they were prosperous. They live simply, they are close to the soil, and so they create wealth. That is the story of the Ukrainian. You can find them between the lakes and north of Winnipeg where they were put into a country of wilderness, of swamp and poplar and stony ridge, a country in which I do not believe any people, even the sturdy French-Qanadian frontiersmen could have lived under the circumstances. But these people have lived there, and it was a great mistake, in my opinion, that they were ever compelled to settle in that part of the country. It was a loss to Canada, and a waste of energy and time to put them in a country that should have been kept as a national preserve for wild animals instead of for these poor people to labour- in. But they have made good, and men in this House can bear me out when I say that wherever these people have gone they have proved successful as settlers. Near Edmonton there are great settlements of them, and they are doing well. I have met many of them, and I want to deal later on with the case of one or two of them by way of illustration. Take also the Germans. I remember Germans north of Indian Head, away across the Qu'Appelle valley, bringing down loads of wood on their sleighs over a haul of thirty or forty miles, and selling it for a few dollars, and hauling their grain over the same distance. Nothing but hardihood and courage and strength of physique could have accomplished this. They made good, however, and to-day are prosperous. I refer to Lemburg and the surrounding districts. Take also the case of the Mennonites. These people have made a garden out of southern Manitoba, and it is a crying shame that a policy of bigotry should have driven from this country some of the best agricultural settlers Canada has ever had.
They are going to stay there.
I sincerely hope so.
Where, in Mexico?
No, in Manitoba; only a few of them are going.

These people came to Canada away back in 1872, and undoubtedly they had an assurance that they would be protected so far as certain of their tenets were concerned. That pledge, I believe, was absolutely and foully violated, and these people out of their strength of conscience and

high resolve, which qualities, whether we agree with their tenets or not, we must admire, felt themselves obliged to leave. They had the courage to leave the land which they had converted into a garden, rather than break faith with those things which they valued more than wealth itself.

Does the hon. member think it bigotry on the part of our government to insist that immigrants shall conform to our educational laws? And does he think it a wise policy to bring people here who will not conform to such laws?
I believe it is the bounden duty of our government to keep its compact. I think that duty is higher than any other.
What compact was violated?

The compact violated was this: Our government sent representatives to these Mennonite people in Russia to induce them to come to Canada. One colony came here, and another went to Kansas. Those who went to the United States settled there on the understanding that they would have to conform to the school laws of the country. The colony that came to western Canada settled there under this compact-that they were not to be called upon for military service, that their religion should be preserved to them, and that they were to be at liberty to educate their children iu their own way, Undoubtedly that compact with the Mennonites was made by the Canadian government. A policy of education in western Canada, dominated very largely by one man, forced a large section of those people either to educate their children in the public schools or to lea#ve Canada. I may say that one-half of the Mennonite colony had pretty well dropped their own school system and were quite willing to adopt the Canadian system, in fact ten or fifteen years would have settled the whole trouble. But some men are impatient, they seem to think that a nation can be made in a day, and that immigrants can be persuaded to surrender their Old Country ideals in favour of Canadian ideals within a very short period of settling here. Well, rather than have our public school system forced on them these people left Canada.

Did the supposed agreement entered into by the government with these Mennonites apply to all of them or only to a certain section that came in a good many years ago? Moreover, has this government

My hon. friend is
diverting me from the thread of my argument. I am not here to discuss whether the provincial government acted rightly or wrongly. I may tell him, however, that education is in the jurisdiction of the provinces.

The hon. gentleman made a serious assertion: he said that a solemn compact had been foully violated. My right hon. friend is entitled to his opinion, but until I am shown something to the contrary I shall adhere to what I have said. A prominent educationalist of Saskatchewan told me recently that night schools are being attended by these men up to thirtj' years of age. I know in the city of Winnipeg these foreign people eagerly seek these educational opportunities. In my constituency I was simply astonished when I became acquainted with these people to find all sorts of halls of learning among them

musical institutions, debating clubs, cultural clubs, surpassing anything that we have among the native bom in the city of Winnipeg. In that city-and the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) no doubt will bear me out-the Ukrainians have a labour hall that cost them some $50,000. As a result of this educational work these people readily become Canadians and are proud of the name. So I would say to the government: Make your immigration policy a wide one, make it an energetic one, throw open your gates and let those who have the hardihood to come to our shores enter and help, and those I have mentioned have helped in the building up of this country.
My hon. friend for St. Lawrenee-St. George (Mr. Marler) spoke of the growth of the United States immediately after the Civil War by reason of their immigration policy. To-day we need such an immigration policy
in a much more marked degree than did the United States at that time. Our people are demanding immigrants. For the last two years I have talked with representative men whenever I had the opportunity upon the question of immigration, and invariably I found they were keen in demanding an energetic immigration policy. I think that is true of our business men, true of a large portion of our agriculturists, and true of many of our Labour leaders-of whom I have the highest possible regard and with whose aims and aspirations I sympathize-many of these leaders to-day are strongly in favour of a proper immigration policy. I think the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) is in favour of an immigration policy, in fact I heard him state so in this House, and I wish he had been more emphatic, but still I think he appreciates that our economic salvation can come only through bringing to this country strong, willing and intelligent workers to develop our resources. By that way, and that way alone, we will get lower taxes and lower freight rates and ultimately lower prices for the commodities that we must consume.

I am glad that that assertion has been made by only a limited number of Progressive members. I am glad that certain members of that party differed, and differed widely, with what I consider were extreme, exaggerated and fantastic reports of farming conditions in western Canada. I appreciate particularly the remarks of the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Lewis) in his very able speech the other day upon this question. I know the district in which he lives; it is a district that for some years has been stricken hardly by climatic conditions. I know the type of people who hav6 lived there-sturdy and energetic and intelligent. In spite of the conditions prevailing there, he was one of those whose mathematics did not lead him to believe that the less was greater than the whole; he saw western Canada as a whole and he gave a fair and faithful report of the conditions existing there. I suggest that I make my speech in my own way; I will come to that in time. The hon. member will make his speech and I will make mine. These were the prices that prevailed in western Canada when there went into that country young men of Ontario, Quebec and the Maritime provinces-bright, intelligent men. They toiled there and in the course of time they became prosperous. They own sections, three-quarter sections, half sections, good buildings; they have been successful because they have been thrifty. The prices of the goods they had to purchase were high; freight rates were high-higher than they are to-day, but up to 1913 these men were prosperous. I have been down in California at a picnic and have seen two or three thousand of them-farmers of western Canada, wintering in California.
Do not overdo it.
I heard it was five thousand, but I will leave it at two.
Were there any other Canadians there but farmers?

Oh, yes. These are the facts. Up to 1913 the West was prosperous, the West did well. It might surprise my friends if I told them that the per capita wealth of the men on the western prairies today is nearly twice that of any other part of this country.
Do you take off the mortgage indebtedness?

I take off all the mortgage indebtedness. In dealing with this question I speak with deepest sympathy for the people of western Canada-and I consider myself one of them. I have seen them go through their struggles. I have seen them as pioneers develop a wilderness into one of the most remarkable agricultural countries on earth. It is a truism that the character of a people is affected by their environment and by their occupation, that it is developed and moulded, as individuals and as groups, by the country in which they are located and by the labour that they must perform. The pioneer is always a sturdy and a courageous man and the western pioneer, going to that land with its wide open spaces, took on something of the bigness of the country. The copper did not exist in the West until the days of Timothy Eaton, and the drinks were three for two bits. Everything was done in a large way. Having taken a quarter section of land, the settler wanted more; he got a half section, and his very virtues of enterprise, ambition and bignes* ultimately became his ruin.

I intend to make it more so before I am done.	*
It is this love stuff I object to.

You must have got over it. You were not always that way.
Then immigration came. The settlers came in and the western man got more land. He bought and he sold, and he sold and he bought. He became a speculator, and we know that the western man assumed a load of debt without any thought of the consequence, just as lightly as a darky would throw a turkey over his shoulder and start off home on Christmas night. The western man contracted liabilities in a free and easy manner without regard for the consequences, like the Irishman who gave a promissory note and said, "Thank God, there is another debt paid." WThat has been the trouble? Speculation, too much credit. My hon. friends over there are .'backing a system whereby the farmer of western Canada can get more credit. I put it to them as individuals, and as a group, is it not a fact that too much credit has been the curse of western Canada? It has been the curse of the city man, I know. Has it not also been the curse of the agriculturist?
Then the war came, with high prices. The farmer of the West flourished, or should have flourished. It is true he paid high wages, but when you consider the price he got for his grain he never paid as low wages as he did then. What was the result? Further speculation. Let me give an instance, and this is a typical instance, not an extraordinary one. Each and all of us in the West can call a case to mind. Down near the town of Morris, some forty miles from the city of Winnipeg in a good section of the country a prosperous Canadian had 960 acres of land. He had it
partially paid for. He had earned it himself from nothing. He decided, good soul, that he would rest, and he bought a house for some four or five thousand dollars in the adjoining town. He sold his farm to some American at a high price, sixty some odd dollars an acre, the farmer receiving a small payment down on it. His brother, who farmed a half section of land some five miles from the town, persuaded the farmer to buy his land. He did so, putting the money he got from his own farm into this house and buying 1,100 acres from his brother from the proceeds of the sale of his farm. Speculating in land, the whole three of them. The war ended, the prices fell. The farmer gets back his farm at Morris. The 960 acres, which were in good condition before the war, come back to him in a dirty and filthy condition. He is not in a position to work the half section he bought from his brother and work the farm too. He has his money in that house and his brother, of course, has lost on the 1,100 acres. There is an instance of two farmers in a 'prosperous condition wiped out by speculation.
Immigration?

The next thing I believe that would be the salvation of the western farmer and of western Canada is not the reduction of tariffs, but a personal economic salvation. It has got to go right back to the farmer himself.
Would not that apply to every class of citizen in Canada just as well?

Absolutely. We have all got to get back to that. Is there bad farming in western Canada? About the worst, I think, in the world. This is a temporary thing in a way. After the Crimean war in old Cam ada and in the old province of Ontario many of the farmers found themselves stranded and in very difficult financial circumstances. Grain was high, as were all other prices, just as was the case during the late war. Farmers bought land for their sons,. and they bought more land; and- the result was that when the war was over they were stranded. The resulting condition w-as a temporary one that gradually

righted itself, and from that time on the province of Ontario has flourished steadily.
The same thing I contend holds in the West. We are to-day in a period of transition in agricultural matters in western Canada. Some ten or twelve years ago the large ranch with its thousands of cattle disappeared. It was unprofitable, uneconomical, and it had to go. The large grain farms of western Canada are also going; there is a transition in process there. There is going to be no more grain mining, no more gambling in grain. The farmer now is not going to work five months in the year; he will be obliged to farm twelve months; he must get acquainted and shake hands twice a day with the homely old milk pail, and he must learn to hear the music of the friendly pig around the place; in other words, he has got to get right down to real genuine farming, and he must get a smaller farm. Does it not appeal to you as ridiculous that the farmer of Ontario, of Quebec, or of Nova Scotia, on a clay land farm not equally as fertile as the wonderful land of western Canada, farms fifty or one hundred acres, while the man in western Canada in order to make a living from a more fertile land must farm a half section, two or three sections and even as high as the American farmer who with his tractor machinery, and so forth, handles eight or ten thousand acres? What is the immediate cause of the financial distress in the West? Well, in that connection I would say, as I have said previously, that this is not a political question or rather it is not a party question. I suppose it is a political question, and for that reason I resent interference by the representatives of foreign nations. But it is not a party question; and I am going to quote from statements made not by members of my own party, but by ministers of the Crown in British Columbia who, of course, are Liberals. The first is a statement made by Hon. E. D. Barrow, Minister of Agriculture in British Columbia. I read from a despatch published in the Vancouver Province of November 23, 1922, dated at Victoria. It says:
Figures showing the extent of the penetration of Japanese and Chinese into the fruit, vegetable and general market gardening industry in British Columbia were given the legislature yesterday by Hon. E. D. Barrow, Minister of Agriculture, in the debate on Mr. Ian Mackenzie's resolution calling for amendment to the B.N.A. Act to give the province power to control oriental ownership of lands or other natural resources and employment in industries connected with them.
Ninety per cent, of the local produce furnished in the city of Vancouver supplied by orientals and 55 per cent, of the potatoes of the province are produced by orientals, Mr. Barrow said.
To present the seriousness of the menace, Mr. Barrow quoted figures which he said were collected two years ago by the department of agriculture in its survey of the yellow peril. This survey showed that there were 14,050 acres of agricultural land owned by Japanese and Chinese and 12,000 acres leased by them.
"That was the condition two years ago and we are satisfied that the acreage held by orientals has been increased since that time," Mr. Barrow said.
At the time of the survey, out of the 4,500 acres in the province devoted to small fruits, the Japanese hold 2.341 acres, or more than 50 per cent. He declared that this added to the problem of the berrygrowers in connection with economical marketing on the prairies.
For truck farming the Chinese own 1,632 acres and lease 8,184 acres, the Japanese own 281 acres and lease 560 acres, a total of 10,097 acres, Mr. Barrow said.
"This is the time to take a definite stand to prevent orientals from acquiring any more of our farm lands," Mr. Barrow went on. "It is now practically impossible to buy any produce not grown by orientals. If the oriental were not producing our vegetables the white

I think the editorial 1 am about to quote is really relevant to the subject under discussion. It summarizes very well the conditions that we are faced with in the city of Vancouver to-day and is entirely relevant, particularly in view of the fact that the government proposes to admit merchants to Canada although other immigration is to be excluded. Now, this editorial from the Vancouver World which, of course, is a government organ, is to the following effect:

The Army of Asiatic Retailers
The figures, printed elsewhere in this paper, showing the extent of the Chinese and Japanese competition in the retail merchandizing and general occupational businesses of this city, will come as a startling revelation to many people.
Within the past year a general branching out of Chinese and Japanese stores has taken place all over the city. There is hardly a business block, either in the down-town section or in the outer districts where the local tradesman is not suffering from the effects of Asiatic competition. But until The World secured the returns from the City Hall records, who for one moment imagined that 1,658 Chinese and Japanese were holding trade licenses within the city limits?
Nor has the worst been reached, by a long way. Six months ago The World pointed out the menace which Would come within a few years from the admissior of last year's army of 1,445 qualified Chinese merchants through the port of Vancouver. Not many of the 1921 class are yet in business. They came armed with the necessary capital to secure entry, but they are still busy learning English, studying Canadian business methods and preparing with patience for the time when they will be able to take their line in the ranks of the commercial contenders for Vancouver's retail trade.
Many of the Chinese retailers are doing business under assumed names. Possibly out of admiration for one of the leaders of the Vancouver bar one Chinese tailor has taken the name of " Charles Wilson." His explanation is that this is his real name " in English." Another. a grocer, has paid a delicate compliment to the Scotch by taking the name of " MacLean." Others are content to take mere company names which sound like the names of Anglo-Saxon concerns, such as " The Royal " and the " North American," etc. But it would surely make the Bard of Avon turn in his grave to see who runs The Stratford Gent's Tailoring Club, or the Stratford gentlemen who patronize it.
To-day the Victoria Chinese are using the strike, picketing and intimidation to prevent the principle of separate schools for Asiatics being introduced there. They and their mouthpieces are demanding that the Asiatic school populace shall be educated on terms of intimacy with the children of white people. Un* doubtedly the equipping of their children with the fullest measure of intimacy with their white competitors in the business affairs of life is the governing factor in the refusal of the Chinese to attend the schools set apart for themselves.
A study of the article referred to will show that there is no line of industry which the evergrowing tide of Asiatic invasion is not prepared to contest with the Anglo-Saxon in this province. The time, has come for some enlightened self-sacrifice on the part of buyers as well as for the utmost efficiency on the part of the tradesmen to meet the situation which is probably destined to reach much more aggravated proportions before relief comes.

I think I have shown that there is something of a real menace facing us, particularly in British Columbia, and I submit that immigration of this class should be excluded from Canada. I was very glad indeed to know that the hon. member who preceded me (Mr. McMurray) agreed with me in this particular. He said that we should encourage to come to Canada those immigrants who have the coinage to work and face hardships, but he would not include in that class the oriental immigrant. Since this matter was before the House last year the agitation for the exclusion
of orientals has been continued in British Columbia. I have before me a number of resolutions which have been passed by organizations at different times since I had the honour to place before this House last session the resolution calling for exclusion. I will not take the time to read these resolutions, but I would say that, irrespective of party, the demand from all classes that these orientals should be excluded from Canada is as strong as ever, and I hope that the Acting Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) will endeavour this year to do something to meet the situation.

I listened with a good deal of amusement and not a little amazement to the address of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. McMurray) this afternoon and evening, but I believe the most amazed member in this House was the hon. Acting Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) himself. I will take up a little later some of the points the hon. member for North Winnipeg dealt with. But at the present time I would like to say a few words with regard to Canada as a country to live in. I believe that it is generally a well-accepted fact that, in so far as Canada is concerned, we have, perhaps, one of the best countries that can be found on the face of the globe. We have a country of large dimensions, and of very extensive natural resources. Those natural resources are so extensive that even the people who are living in Canada to-day do not know a tithe of their extent. Under these circumstances it would be quite natural, of course, for us to expect that immigration to Canada! would be almost spontaneous. But I find myself in a somewhat peculiar position, and that position is simply this, that, so far as the people of Canada are concerned, we must take the condition to-day and discuss it as it exists.
I regret that I had not the opportunity of listening to very much of this debate. I have been engaged in the special
10 p.m. committee on Agriculture looking into agricultural conditions and consequently I may perhaps repeat some of the arguments that have been used and if so, I will have to ask the pardon of the House! It is proposed by the Acting Minister of Immigration on behalf of the government to increase the immigration grant in the effort to induce people to come to Canada, and I understand the bulk of the money is going to be spent in an endeavour to bring to this country farmers, agricultural labourers and domestic servants. In so far as the two latter classes are concerned, I believe the country can well afford to accept quite a few immigrants who
