come as farm help, that we can also afford to accept a number of domestics but I find my* self in somewhat of a disagreement with those who propose to bring in people who will immediately go on the land. First of all let me say that I am not very well acquainted with conditions in the East, and consequently I must speak of that part of the country which I know best-western Canada.
We have heard many speeches in this House with regard to conditions in the West. We have heard some addresses which to all intents and purposes intimated to members of this House that conditions in western Canada were not nearly as bad as they were painted, but I may say that I listened to the address of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) some few days ago and I noticed that the press of this country got after him very severely because he chose to tell the truth as he knew it in this House. I am fairly well acquainted with the conditions in the district in which that hon. member lives, and if I can add anything to what he has stated, I would say that the hon. member told a part of the truth and not all of it. If he had told the conditions as they really exist in that part ' of the country, I believe the members of this House would be still more amazed than they were at what he said- I believe it is generally understood, so far as Canada is concerned, that we have in our cities, towns and villages, a greater population than conditions at the present time could justify. I noticed in one of the Ottawa papers the other day a statement by Mayor Plant that 20 per cent of the citizens of Ottawa have received some assistance during this last winter. That condition is more or less prevalent throughout the whole of Canada, and, it consequently is convincing evidence of the inadvisability of bringing in more people who would settle in the cities, towns and villages, and of the wisdom of bringing people who would settle on the land and become farm labourers or domestic servants.
We heard a good deal about agriculture during the war. Hon. members of this House will remember how the government of the day did everything in their power to induce the farmers throughout the length and breadth of Canada to produce and produce some more, and no doubt the farmers of Canada did all in their power to produce all they possibly could. As a matter of fact, some of the farmers in Canada got into financial difficulties because they undertook to produce more than their capital would allow them to produce efficiently. But the point I want to bring before the House is this: Hon. members will remember that during the war the people of

Canada recognized the fact-and I believe it was stated on more than one occasion on the floor of this House-that agriculture was the backbone of Canada. I have here a summary of Canadian trade for the eleven months ending February 28, 1923, and I wish to call the attention of the committee to some of the items contained therein. If we look down the export column for that period we shall find that Canada exported altogether $854,893,844 worth of goods. The amount of agricultural products exported included the following items: First, we have agricultural and vegetable products, mainly foods, totalling $363,615,713; next, agricultural and vegetable products other than foods, $21,479,441; and there is another item, animals and animal products, amounting to $126,922,203.
Now, Mr. Chairman, all these products spring first of all from the farm. True, there are included in some of the items agricultural products which are partly manufactured, such as flour, and other articles which undergo some finishing process, such as bacon, etc. But the point I want to drive home is this, that agriculture as the basic industry of the country provided exports during that eleven months amounting to a total of $512,017,357, leaving for all exports of all other classes of commodities produced in Canada only $342,876,487. There is something else I would bring closely to the attention of the committee. Let us take fibres, textiles and textile products. During the eleven months I have mentioned Canada has exported $6,946,047 worth of these products. I hope that the House will bear these figures in mind, because they are important. Obviously therefore there seems to be no question about the fact that agriculture is the backbone of Canada; but, if I might say so, I think that Canada's backbone is broken and broken badly.
I have some information here which I might give to the committee relating to the economic conditions of western Canada, and I speak of a part of the country that I know very well. While it is admitted that during the past years we have had a dry area in western Canada, yet in the greater portion of the West we have had fairly good crops; and I do know from actual experience, in discussing various matters with farmers qf western Canada, that even in those parts of the country where the people enjoyed good crops they seem to be as badly in debt as are the people where there were practically no crops at all. I do not know what the idea of the minister or the government can be in bringing more people into the country to go on the land. I cannot comprehend the reason at all. I do not know whether it is for the

purpose of increasing the population or in order to increase production. No doubt the object is mainly to increase production, and if that is the case I desire to submit to the committee some evidence that has been given before the special committee on Agriculture, so that we may see whether we can afford to produce much more agricultural commodities than we are doing now.
The special committee, of which I happen to be a member, has taken a good deal of evidence and it appears, practically from every witness that has come before the committee, that the conditions in regard to agriculture are deplorable not only in the West but in the East as well; and even in Quebec the conditions appear to be as bad as they are in western Canada. The other day we had a witness from Montreal who stated that the farmers of Quebec are up in arms because they receive so little for their produce notwithstanding that they have to pay high prices for the things which they must have in order to produce farm products.
The committee will remember that at the last session of parliament we passed an act for the purpose of grading hogs, and the reason given by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) for the passing of that act was its necessity in order that we might get a class of hog grown in Canada from which we could produce what he called "Wiltshire sides" that could be sold to advantage in Great Britain. I do not know for what reason, but I am told that that act has never been enforced in eastern Canada; it has been applied only in the West. Now, I do not know that the Minister of Agriculture under the act was allowed to discriminate as between the East and the West in its application, and whatever reason he may have had for hot putting it into force in eastern Canada is totally unknown to me. Perhaps the Mininster of Agriculture may some time in the future explain this discrimination. The fact remains, however, that the real idea behind that act was for us to produce such a class of bacon hog in Canada as would enable us to compete with other bacon-producing countries in the world for the market in Great Britain. We were told that that was practically the only market available for bacon products, and consequently we must produce that kind of bacon which was desired there. I believe that the members of the committee will admit with me that we have produced what is termed "select bacon hogs." We have produced the best hog it is possible to produce in this or any other country. But what is the situation? We find that when the packing houses have taken the
select hogs from our farmers and have properly graded them, when they have cured them and cut them up into Wiltshire sides, they sell that bacon in Great Britain at a loss. Mr. McLean, the Secretary-Treasurer of the Harris Abattoir in Toronto, appeared before the committee the other day and he was asked at what price they were selling this Wiltshire bacon in Great Britain. I quote from the evidence:
By the Chairman:
Q. Just let me ask you this question. What are you selling bacon for in England at the present time?-A. I should say that the average price of Canadian bacon sold in England last week was about 80 shillings per 112 pounds.
If we figure this out in Canadian money we find that the price is about 18 cents per pound for the best bacon Canada can produce. I might explain to the committee that this bacon is merely cured; it is not smoked. When it gets into Great Britain the people who get it smoke it and place it on the market. But the most amazing part of Mr. McLean's statement was that it cost the Harris Abattoir 96 shillings to produce that bacon which was sold for 80 shillings in Great Britain, or in other words, a loss of 16 shillings on every 112 pounds sold on the British market. The question is, how long can we continue to feed Great Britain at a loss with our best farm products? How long can that continue; and in view of that, would it be advisable to ask the people of Great Britain or the United States to come to Canada and Btart farming? Could we ask them to come here and farm in order to produce the best class of bacon so that it. might be sold in the British market at a lower price than it is sold for in Canada?
Two or three ciays after Mr. McLean had given his evidence I looked up one of the Calgary newspapers. As hon. members know, we have a big packing plant in Calgary, which is one of the best in the country. I noticed that they were advertising the best bacon at 45 cents and best hams at 33 cents per pound. At the same time they were selling bacon in Great Britain at 18 cents a pound. I maintain that such a condition of affairs should not be allowed to continue any longer than can possibly be prevented, and until it is eliminated it seems to me to be futile to ask people to come to this country to engage in farming. I would suggest to the Acting Minister of Immigration that he might better spend some of this money which he is asking for immigration in advertising in the Old Country papers something along these lines:
If you purpose coming to Canada to farm, don't; stay in Great Britain, because we will feed you cheaper there than here in Canada.

That is not the only farm product, Mr. Chairman, that we are selling in Great Britain at a loss. Here is another very substantial item. We had before that special committee the secretary-treasurer of the Millers' Association of Canada, comprising the millers of Ontario and Quebec. This gentleman stated that wheat ground in Canada and shipped as flour to Great Britain was being charged from 2 to 5 cents per 100 pounds more in freight than the flour of wheat ground in United States mills. It seemed that it made no difference whether the boats were of British or Canadian registry, providing they sailed from a United States port they carried flour ground in United States mills that much cheaper than they would carry Canadian-ground flour. But the most amazing statement he made was when he was asked whether the mills that he represented were selling flour in Great Britain at a lower price than in Canada. He answered, "Absolutely, relatively we are selling flour in Great Britain at a lower price than we are selling it in Canada." And he had a most ingenious excuse to offer by way of explanation. He said, "If we were supplying the Canadian market alone we could only run our mills about 50 per cent of the time; by running our mills full time, even if we have to sell our flour at a lower price in Great Britain than we receive in Canada, this lower price provides a little profit towards meeting our overhead expenses. Consequently we do sell flour in Great Britain at a lower price than here." Now, it seems to me there is something radically wrong with any system that will permit the products of the Canadian farm and the Canadian mill being sold abroad at a lower price than what they can be obtained for at home, and I trust, Mr. Chairman, that the special committee will have some substantial recommendations to make to this House, and I hope that if those recommendations have any virtue they will be incorporated in legislation.
The hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. McMurray) dealt quite lavishly with conditions in western Canada, and told us that it was possible to get all the immigrants we require from continental Europe, and that they would naturally make the very best settlers. As far as I am concerned, I should like to say that if those people care to come here on their own initiative I would not wish to keep them out, but I do say that we farmers of western Canada-and I believe I may speak for the farmers of the East as well- have no desire to compete against this class of farm labour. We do not wish to have to accept their standard of living, and consequently we are opposed to any great influx of such immi-

grants. This very important fact must be remembered, that to-day we find a very much higher standard of living in our urban centres than in our rural, and this is really the reason why so many of our young people, and even of our older people, are being attracted to our cities, towns and villages. If we are going to keep our people on the land the living conditions in rural Canada should be made just as good as they are in the urban centres.
With regard to wheat production, the hon. member for North Winnipeg seemed to think that all we had to do in western Canada was to produce as much as we possibly could and we were bound to be successful. But there is such a thing, Mr. Chairman, as cost of production. If we take into consideration our cost of production we find that invariably there is quite a discrepancy between this cost and the price we receive for our products. Until the report and evidence have been laid upon the table, it is irregular to refer to them in debate or to put questions in reference to the proceedings of the committee.
I would therefore ask the hon. member to refrain from quoting from the report of a committee which is at present sitting.

I will not quote the figures, then, Mr. Chairman, but I think I shall be quite within the rules if I give a summary of the results. This young man made a study of agricultural conditions in Manitoba. He took three specific points and got the farmers to keep exact cost accounts. After these accounts had been finally analyzed it was found that the cost of producing wheat at those three points was more, and in some cases very much more, than the farmers received for the product. In other words, the wheat was produced at a loss. Later in the session the House may have an opportunity of getting the actual figures, and it will then be found that my summary is borne out by the evidence. If we farmers in western Canada are producing our wheat and other products at a loss, what is the sense of bringing other people here to produce still more products to be sold at a still greater loss? Of course, it is well understood that so far as the price of our wheat is concerned it is set by the Liverpool market. Therefore our only remedy is to reduce the cost of production.

Supply-Immigration
190?
That is where the salvation of the Canadian farmers seems to lie in my judgment.
For the last forty or fifty years we have had a fiscal policy which seems to be based upon the principle that those industries which may be termed secondary must receive extra consideration. That is to say, these industries which are based on our primary industries receive protection, but our primary industries receive no protection whatsoever. Consequently we have to meet the competition of the world, and this coupled with the fact that our home manufacturers are enabled to set the price of their products means that what we must buy is at a price out of proportion to what we receive for that which we have to sell. The policy of the government seems to be to adopt immigration as a cure for the depression that we have in Canada at present. I remember that -when I was a young boy I used to go to fairs, and there we would see gentlemen who were selling salves and lotions which they -claimed were a cure for all diseases. It is possible that these remedies did do some good; but while they might heal a running sore for the time being it was invariably the case that the disease would break out in some other part of the body, so that the patient would have to consult a physician or surgeon before actual relief was obtained. No doubt the skilled surgeon, instead of using salves and lotions, would use the knife and with a few deft strokes cut out the offending part and afford real and lasting relief to the patient. We used to call the gentlemen who sold these salves and pills, "quack doctors"; and it seems to me that the remedy the government proposes for the present depression- immigration-is a quack remedy that will not satisfy the people of Canada any more than the remedies advocated by the quack doctors relieved their physical ills. I do not know whether the minister would give a name to the remedy which he proposes; he might call it "immigration lotion," to be well rubbed in -something of that description. I am satisfied, however, that it will not be a cure for the economic disease from which we are suffering at the present; some more specific remedy will have to be applied.
I would like to make a few suggestions for the consideration of the government as to what I believe would be advisable in the interests of Canada as a whole, and more particularly in the interests of the farmers. The first thing I regard as necessary is a reduction in the cost of living, that is, a lowering of the cost of the things we must have in order to exist. The prices of agricultural products have come down very substantially; as a matter of fact many of our products are down to the basis of pre-war figures, but we find on looking over the list of other things that we must buy, such as boots, shoes, clothing of all descriptions, furniture, etc., that the prices of these articles are high in comparison with the prices of agricultural products. I believe, therefore, that the House would be well advised to consider seriously ways and means whereby the cost of these commodities may be greatly reduced.
Our greatest disability in western Canada at the present time is lack of proper line of credit. I have nothing to say against the banks so far as the amount of credit they are giving is concerned, but hon. members will realize that the banks are not in the business of giving long-term loans; they are organized only for the purpose of giving short-term loans. While bank loans or bank credits, therefore, may be fairly satisfactory for seasonable loans they are not at all satisfactory for long-term loans. Our present long-term loan system is very expensive. We can get loans from the mortgage companies for a term of five years-sometimes we can get ten years -at a rate of interest of about 8 or 9 per cent. In the first place, agriculture cannot pay as high a rate of interest as 8 or 9 per cent, so that some means will have to be found whereby we can get cheaper money for long-term loans. When a farmer gets a loan of $1,000 on his quarter-section of land from a mortgage company, he finds that when he goes to the bank to get the proceeds there is coming ' to him only $940 or $950 instead of $1,000. In other words, it has cost anywhere from $40 to $60 to have that loan put through; the amount which he actually receives is reduced by that sum, and on the top of that he pays 8 or 9 per cent interest. But that is not all. If at the end of the five years he is incapable of paying off the loan, he has to incur practically the same expense that he incurred originally, in order to have it renewed. It seems to me that in any country which claims to be an agricultural country the first thing to do is to provide what we would call long term rural credits at reasonable rates of interest. I say that one of our greatest disabilities at present is our high interest rates. I trust, therefore, that before the session is concluded the House will see its way clear to make some provision along these lines.
I have said that we are paying too much for the things we must have in order to produce. I would like to see, when the budget comes down, a [DOT] substantial reduction in the tariff duties. We are not asking the House or the government to take off the duties entirely. but a substantial all-round reduction

Supply-Immigration

would, I believe, be one of the best things that could happen to Canada. If there was a little more competition from outside sources we could realize the possibility of getting at a lower price the commodities that we must have in order to live.
A good deal has been said about the conditions in Quebec, which has been held up as a province where everybody is prosperous, particularly the farmer. When the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) came before the House with his estimates, he gave us a brief outline of his travels during last summer and he held up the province of Quebec, so far as agriculture was concerned, as the banner province of Canada. But we have had quite a number of witnesses from that province who seem to think that agriculture in Quebec is just about as badly off as it is in any other province, and that there is just as much dissatisfaction among the farmers . there as there is among the farmers of the West.
We have in the past been spending millions of money to bring people to this country. We have held out-to them the possibility of making a livelihood here, but circumstances and conditions which now prevail have placed them in a very precarious financial position. In view of the fact that these people have come here at the invitation of the Canadian government on behalf of the Canadian people, it seems to me that our first duty is to look after those who are already here. When we have made conditions livable for those who are now in Canada, that will be time enough to launch out upon a substantial immigration policy. Let me repeat, the duty of this House and the duty of Canada is to the people who are now here. I am convinced, of course, of the fact that immigration eventually will have to increase before Canada can ever enjoy that measure of prosperity that she should have, but our first duty, it seems to me, is to take cognizance of the conditions that confront us now and find a remedy, if possible, for those conditions. When we have found the proper remedies for the unfortunate condition that we have at the present time, there is no doubt in my mind that Canada will not have to spend very much money to induce people to come to this country. The moment people throughout the world realize that Canada is enjoying a substantial measure of prosperity we shall get all the immigrants we require without spending very much money.
